hook.text: First place is on the line in the final round at Hastings. Then one pawn becomes a queen, and the whole board catches fire.

yt_hook: First Place Was On The Line
yt_detail: Alekhine trusts a passed pawn over material
title: Final-Round Firestorm
description: Efim Bogoljubov and Alexander Alekhine meet in round 10 at Hastings 1922, with the tournament still hanging in the balance. The event was a six-player double round-robin held from 9 to 21 September 1922. Watch how Alekhine turns cramped tension into a passed-pawn storm and a technical endgame. Alekhine later called this one of the most brilliant tournament games of his career, and Irving Chernev ranked it as the finest game of chess ever played.

segments.text: Hastings, September nineteen twenty-two. Efim Bogoljubov has White, Alexander Alekhine has Black, and this is round ten, the final round of a six-player double round-robin. First place is still at stake, five years before Alekhine becomes world champion.
White starts: {{m:1}}. Black immediately chooses a fighting setup: {{m:2}}. {{s:7}} The pieces come out, and the game already has a sharp edge. Black shows the first sting: {{m:8}}.
{{s:10}} The early bishop trade gives White a choice. White chooses: {{m:11}}. {{s:16}} Both kings are safe, and the center is still waiting to open.
White starts probing: {{m:17}}. Black calmly replies: {{m:18}}. {{s:20}} The center is challenged, and the quiet opening is over.
White plays solidly: {{m:21}}. {{s:24}} Black's queen is ready to switch wings. The real signal comes next: {{m:26}}. The kingside is no longer quiet, and Black jumps in: {{m:28}}.

White increases the kingside tension: {{m:29}}. Black finishes an important regrouping: {{m:30}}. Now comes the first real slip, the engine says White's choice gives Black a clear pull: {{m:31}}. Black answers simply: {{m:32}}.
White tries to hold space: {{m:33}}. Black finds the reply the engine wanted: {{m:34}}. Suddenly White's pieces are defending squares, not creating threats.
{{s:36}} The position tightens, and White is pushed backward. White has to step back: {{m:37}}. Black locks in the structure: {{m:38}}. {{s:40}} The black pieces keep rotating toward better squares.

White looks for space on the queenside: {{m:41}}. Black brings another knight into the fight: {{m:42}}. {{s:46}} White keeps shuffling defenders, while Black's queen returns to keep pressure everywhere.
White looks active: {{m:47}}. But Black opens the queenside: {{m:48}}. After the recapture, Black grabs another target: {{m:50}}. {{s:52}} The engine now shows Black with a winning edge.

White's knights circle back, trying to cover everything: {{m:53}}. Black expands again: {{m:54}}. Then the knight lands deep in White's camp: {{m:56}}. The squeeze is no longer just positional, it is tactical.

White grabs material: {{m:57}}. Black keeps pushing: {{m:58}}. White goes for the most tempting material: {{m:59}}. Now Black can chase material, or trust the passer, what would you do? {{p}} Black chooses the passer: {{m:60}}.

White keeps taking on the back rank: {{m:61}}. Black drives the pawn one step from promotion: {{m:62}}. White checks: {{m:63}}, and Black answers: {{m:64}}. One pawn is ready to become a queen, can you find Black's cleanest continuation? {{p}} Here it is: {{m:66}}.
White tries to bottle up the new queen: {{m:67}}. Black jumps into the back rank: {{m:68}}. White's rook seeks counterplay: {{m:69}}, but Black cleans up: {{m:70}}.
The rook invades: {{m:71}}. Black sets a bishop trap: {{m:72}}. White takes it: {{m:73}}, and Black removes the rook: {{m:74}}. Then Black's knight check tears away more cover: {{m:76}}.

White gives up the bishop: {{m:77}}. Black recaptures and keeps a dangerous pawn alive: {{m:78}}. White grabs on the kingside: {{m:79}}, and Black invades with the queen: {{m:80}}. {{s:82}} Both kings still have work to do.

White throws another pawn forward: {{m:83}}. Black steps out of danger: {{m:84}}. White tries to open lines: {{m:85}}, and the black queen takes over the center: {{m:88}}. The passed pawn rushes on: {{m:89}}, but Black removes it: {{m:90}}.

White's last try is a kingside passer: {{m:91}}. Black wipes it out: {{m:92}}. White brings the rook back: {{m:93}}, but Black's queen penetrates: {{m:94}}. The rooks vanish, and another pawn becomes a queen: {{m:98}}.
White takes that queen off the board: {{m:99}}. But the pawn ending is already hopeless: {{m:100}}. The kings walk in: {{m:102}}. Black's king reaches the center: {{m:104}}.

White's king steps forward: {{m:105}}, and Black answers: {{m:106}}. Bogoljubov realized his position was lost, and resigned. With this win, Alekhine finished first with seven and a half out of ten, half a point ahead of Akiba Rubinstein, and he later called this one of the most brilliant tournament games of his career. Irving Chernev ranked it as the finest game of chess ever played.
